# Configure rolebox

Use this guide for the rolebox version that shipped it. Read the relevant local
reference instead of searching rolebox implementation files. Host tools can have
an MCP prefix; use the names and schemas actually registered in the session.

## Choose the configuration surface

| Goal | Read |
| --- | --- |
| Locate configuration, install/sync roles, map Codex native agents, set model aliases, project defaults or automatic role activation | [Configuration and hosts](references/configuration.md) |
| Author `role.yaml`, choose models, restrict tools, configure memory or private subagents | [Roles](references/roles.md) |
| Add skills, reusable functions, activation rules or reference documents | [Assets and functions](references/assets.md) |
| Dispatch work, declare outcome graphs, set worker budgets or form a role team | [Orchestration](references/orchestration.md) |
| Configure hooks, error recovery, Copilot, notifications, browser/desktop access or LSP | [Runtime features](references/runtime.md) |

## Apply a change

1. Identify the active harness and workspace. Resolve environment overrides before
   selecting a file. A workspace `rolebox/` directory takes precedence over the
   harness's `rolebox/` directory; these trees are not merged.
2. Read the existing configuration and the relevant reference. Keep unrelated
   values. A directory name is a role ID; `name` is its display name.
3. Write the smallest supported configuration. Use an installed provider/model ID
   or configure an alias; an alias does not install a provider or credentials.
4. Verify YAML/JSON parsing and any referenced files, then reload/restart the host
   and inspect role/tool discovery. Use `asset_validate` when available for role
   resources. Its result does not validate every runtime option or host policy.
5. Report the changed files, how to activate the behavior, and what was actually
   verified. A setting being accepted by a parser does not prove it is effective.

`rolebox-config` is a global built-in skill, available even before any roles are
installed. Installation syncs it to existing harness homes; host startup and
`rolebox sync <target>` repair its link as well. Regular files/directories at the
destination are preserved. If installation scripts were disabled or a host was
installed later, run the sync command and restart that host for skill discovery.

For Codex, read Configuration, Roles and Orchestration together: native public-agent
discovery, private graph workers and MCP tool discovery have different scopes.
Execution requires host-supplied thread/sandbox metadata; a generated file or tool
schema alone does not establish that capability.

Do not edit this installed skill to configure a role: it links into the package
and updates with rolebox. Put user configuration in the locations described by
the references. Configure only the task the user authorized; enabling a workflow
does not grant permission for external actions or override host permissions.

# Computer use

You are driving the user's real desktop. Nothing you deliver can be taken back:
a click, a keystroke or a typed string that reached an application is already
part of the desktop's state. Work slowly, observe before every action, and stop
when you are unsure.

## The loop: observe -> act -> verify

**1. Observe.** Find the target before you touch anything.

- `computer_windows({app?})` lists the visible windows with the id this OS
  uses. Pass `app` to narrow the list — it matches a case-insensitive substring
  of the window owner's name on macOS, of the window title on X11, and of the
  process name or the title on Windows. On macOS a filter that matches nothing is
  an error, not an empty list; on X11 and Windows it lists nothing, so an empty
  answer there means the filter matched no window. On macOS the ids come from the
  window server, so they are real CGWindowIDs that
  `computer_screenshot({window_id})` accepts; the titles need Screen Recording
  and are empty without it.
- `computer_screenshot({window_id?, region?, display?})` captures the screen,
  one window or one rectangle as a PNG. Pass at most one target: `window_id`,
  `region` and `display` are mutually exclusive, and on macOS a `region` cannot
  be combined with `display` (macOS counts displays from 1). The image comes
  back to you on an image-capable route and is also saved under
  `.rolebox/computer/` in the workspace.

The screenshot is in **device pixels**, which are not the coordinates the input
tools take: a 2x retina capture of a 1512x982 screen comes back 3024x1964 px
with `metadata.pixel_scale` 2, and the result's text repeats the scale. **Divide
any x/y you read off the image by `pixel_scale`** before `computer_click` or
`computer_move` — an unconverted pixel coordinate lands at twice the intended
offset. When you need to compute a click position, prefer a full-screen or
`region` capture: a `window_id` capture is a cropped frame with no screen origin.

Read what the screenshot actually shows. Do not plan a click from memory of an
earlier screenshot.

**2. Act.** Use the smallest gesture that moves the task forward.

- `computer_click({x, y, button?, clicks?, window_id?})` — one button at one
  point in screen coordinates, so divide the pixel coordinates you read off a
  screenshot by its `pixel_scale` first. `window_id` targets one X11 window;
  macOS and Windows send input to the focused window instead.
- `computer_move({x, y})` — move the pointer to a screen coordinate without
  clicking.
- `computer_type({text, window_id?})` — type text into the focused window. A
  newline presses Return. The text is never echoed back into the transcript.
- `computer_key({keys, window_id?})` — press one key with optional modifiers,
  modifiers first: `["cmd", "shift", "t"]`, `["ctrl", "c"]`, `["Return"]`.

Type into a window only after you have focused it with a click or a key press.

**3. Verify.** Take a fresh `computer_screenshot` after every meaningful action
and check that the screen changed the way you intended. If it did not, do not
repeat the same gesture blindly — re-observe, work out what the screen is
telling you, and adjust.

## Rehearse with dry_run first

Every tool accepts `dry_run: true`. It returns the exact command the tool would
spawn as JSON (`argv`, `windowsVerbatimArguments`, and `script` for an
interpreter command) and executes nothing.

Rehearse whenever the gesture is risky or the target is uncertain:

- a click that would submit a form, send a message or confirm a dialog
- a `computer_type` containing credentials, a shell command or a URL
- a `computer_key` combination whose effect you cannot predict

`dry_run` shows you the coordinates, the window id, the button and the click
count that would really be used. If the plan does not match what you intended,
fix the arguments and rehearse again — never "try it and see".

## Permissions: check, do not guess

`computer_permissions({dry_run?, request?})` reports whether this system
reports synthesized input as permitted right now and names the grant to fix when
it does not.

- On macOS, call it before your first gesture. Input goes through System Events
  and needs **Accessibility** permission for the terminal or agent process that
  launched the host; screenshots — and the window *titles* in
  `computer_windows` — need **Screen Recording**. The window list itself needs
  neither: its ids come from the window server. Installing rolebox with npm
  grants none of these.
- **Pass `request: true` to ask the OS for the grant instead of only reporting
  it.** On macOS that makes the system show its Accessibility dialog (and
  registers the app in System Settings) rather than answering silently. The
  dialog appears once per application; approve it.
- **A restart is needed after granting.** The grant goes to the process that
  launched the host, so the host must be restarted before input works — then call
  `computer_permissions` again and confirm it reports the grant before you retry
  the gesture.
- Follow the remediation text the tool returns verbatim — it names the exact
  System Settings pane and the process that must be granted, and `request: true`
  can open the same flow through the OS prompt.
- If a gesture fails with a permission error, call `computer_permissions` and
  report what it says to the user. Do not retry the same gesture in a loop.

## When to stop and ask the user

Stop, report what you observed, and ask before continuing when:

- `computer_permissions` reports that input is not permitted, or the session is
  Wayland (rolebox drives X11 only) or otherwise unsupported;
- the screen does not show what you expected — a different window is focused, a
  dialog you did not anticipate is open, or the desktop changed between calls
  (the desktop is shared; another person or program can move it);
- the next step would destroy data, install or remove software, change system
  settings, send a message, make a payment, or enter credentials;
- you have verified the same action twice and the screen still has not changed.

Prefer one careful verified step over a long unverified sequence.

# rolebox

Turn one coding agent into a configured engineering team.
Specialist YAML roles with their own prompts, models, skills and permissions — run as explicit graphs, with memory that survives the session.

One plugin for opencode, pi, dsh and Codex.

The role picker, opened from the composer: Filter roles searches the 18 loaded roles, each row a display name and a one-line description, and the header names the current selection, Base agent.

What it is · See it work · Install · Roles · What you get · Engine · CLI · Docs

--- ## What it is A general coding agent is one agent with one prompt. rolebox turns it into *your* configured team: specialists defined in YAML, each with its own prompt, model, skills and permissions, working the same task together. What they learn survives the session — decisions, conventions and lessons persist in memory and come back at the next session start. On DSH, roles can collaborate through [persistent peer teams](docs/team-work.md): invite complementary specialists, exchange events, claim tasks, and continue work across turns. Team execution on other hosts is deferred. Structured workflows use **declared** graphs: `graph_declare` names each node's agent, brief, and permitted outcomes; the host dispatches entry nodes and workers settle them with `graph_submit_outcome`. Graph nodes advance only through accepted outcomes, with bounded loops and inspectable state. **At a glance** - **Roles** — 18 specialists on the public [oh-my-role registry](https://github.com/EricMoin/oh-my-role), or write your own in one YAML file. - **Runtime** — the graph v3 outcome protocol: declared nodes and edges, accepted outcomes, bounded repair loops. - **Memory** — SQLite + FTS5, auto-injected at session start and searchable from the CLI. - **Tools** — 32 `lsp_*` language-server tools, `hashline_*` edits anchored to content hashes, skills, references, custom functions and hooks. - **Desktop** — a 12-tool `computer_*` family: `computer_screenshot`, `computer_windows`, `computer_displays`, `computer_focus`, `computer_click`, `computer_move`, `computer_scroll`, `computer_drag`, `computer_type`, `computer_key`, `computer_status`, `computer_permissions`. - **Browser** — a [23-tool `browse_*` family](docs/browser-use.md) for semantic web-page automation: `browse_status`, `browse_open`, `browse_snapshot`, `browse_read`, `browse_click`, `browse_drag`, `browse_type`, `browse_press`, `browse_select`, `browse_hover`, `browse_scroll`, `browse_wait`, `browse_eval`, `browse_screenshot`, `browse_upload`, `browse_downloads`, `browse_dialog`, `browse_tabs`, `browse_history`, `browse_console`, `browse_network`, `browse_cookies`, `browse_close`. Gated by `browseUse`; actions need the optional Playwright peer (`npm install playwright`, then `npx playwright install chromium`). - **Visibility** — the dsh Rolebox monitor pane, the `rolebox monitor` TUI, and channel-filtered logs. --- ## See it work Every screenshot in this README was captured from a live dsh session on a demo workspace. Each caption states only what that capture shows. ### 1 · Every loaded role, on one page

Settings → Rolebox: the 18 roles that loaded, each with its slug, description and declared tool policy.

Each card carries the display name, the slug at the right (`ai-designer`, `apk-reverse-engineer`, `comment-writer` in the capture), a description paragraph, then three label/value rows — **Model**, **Mode**, **Max steps** — and a `Tool policy:` footer. In this capture every visible card reads Model `default`, Mode `primary`, Max steps `not set` and `Tool policy: none declared`; **no card names a source or origin path**. The header carries the `18 roles` badge, the `Refresh`, `Reload roles` and `Open monitor` buttons, and a right-aligned `Loaded 18 roles · ` line recording when the load happened. ### 2 · Work is declared as a graph, not prompted node by node

The TypeScript Engineer loads its own skill, reads the protocol reference, and declares the work with graph_declare.

The role does not do the work inline. It inspects the repo and records a baseline before editing — the sample project’s test command → 4 pass / 0 fail, `tsc --noEmit` → exit 0 — then names one real design point: `Task` has no completion state at all, so `removeCompleted()` needs one. It takes the minimal, backward-compatible reading — an optional `completed?: boolean` on `Task` plus `removeCompleted(): number` returning the removed count — and passes that decision to the worker explicitly. It then declares `graph_declare · taskstore-remove-completed` and yields the turn so the engine can schedule it. The plan names exactly two nodes and one bounded repair round: - **`change`** (`change-applier`) — implement `removeCompleted(): number` in `src/store.ts`, add the optional `completed?: boolean` field to `Task` in `src/task.ts`, add a focused test in `tests/task.test.ts`, and run the sample project’s test command and `tsc --noEmit`. - **`review`** (`verification`, independent) — read the actual files and re-run both checks against the same baseline. The turn closes on the declaration being started (`start.kind: started`, phase `executing`, node `change` dispatched). The capture states no execution budget. ### 3 · Independent verification, then reconciliation

Accepted results come back; the parent reconciles them, re-runs the checks itself, and states what was verified and what remains uncertain.

Both nodes ran in their own sessions, and the verifying node is not the node that wrote the code. The closing synthesis reports the test coverage — `tests/task.test.ts:35-61`, importing `TaskStore` at line 4 — as two behavior tests: a mixed store that removes exactly the completed entry and returns `1` while non-completed entries and `get`/`count`/`all` stay consistent, and a no-op path that returns `0` with the store deep-equal to a pre-call snapshot. A `Checks` table sets each check against its baseline: the sample project’s test command went from `4 pass / 0 fail` to `6 pass / 0 fail, 17 expect() calls, exit 0`, and `tsc --noEmit` stayed at `exit 0` (TypeScript 6.0.3). description: Execute the approved plan with per-step verification, continue until all steps done
phase: execute
priority: 20
consumes: plan
params:
  plan: ""
requires_evidence: [lsp_diagnostics, test]
continue_max: 30
observe:
  - on: tool_after
    tool: todowrite
    sync_todos: true
  - on: activate
    inject: "If {plan} param is set, read .rolebox/plans/{plan}.md to find your resume point. If no plan artifact was injected via consumes, the plan file IS your source of truth."
continue_until:
  all: [plan_todos_complete, evidence_met]
---

You are now in EXECUTION mode. You have a plan (explicit or implied). Implement it systematically.

## Cross-Session Resume

When activated in a fresh session (no plan artifact injected via `consumes`), follow this resume protocol:

### 1. Locate the Plan

- If `{plan}` param is set: read `.rolebox/plans/{plan}.md`
- If `{plan}` is empty: glob `.rolebox/plans/*.md`, filter for files containing `- [ ]` (unchecked steps)
  - Single match → auto-select it
  - Multiple matches → list them and ask the user which to resume
  - No matches → tell the user "No incomplete plans found. Use |plan| to create one."

### 2. Determine Resume Point

Parse the plan file:
- Lines matching `- [x]` → already completed, skip
- First line matching `- [ ]` → this is your starting point
- Report to the user: "Resuming plan '{name}' from step N (steps 1–M already complete)"

### 3. Execute with Checkpoint

For each step you complete:
1. Do the work (same as normal execution below)
2. Verify it passed
3. **Flip the checkbox**: use the Edit tool to change that step's `- [ ]` to `- [x]` in `.rolebox/plans/{plan}.md`
4. This edit IS the persistent progress — it survives session restarts

### 4. Single-Session Mode (backward compat)

If a plan artifact WAS injected (normal `plan` → transition → `execute` flow within one session), work from the artifact as before. Still flip checkboxes in the plan file if one exists at `.rolebox/plans/`.

## Process

### 1. Work Step by Step

For each step:

- Complete it fully before moving on
- Don't skip ahead or combine unrelated steps
- If the plan proves wrong mid-execution, stop. State what changed. Propose revision.

### 2. Verify After Each Change

After every file edit or meaningful action, verify with your tools:

- **lsp_diagnostics** on changed files — no new errors introduced
- **Bash** to run build/test commands if the project has them
- **Read** the changed file to confirm the edit landed correctly
- **Grep** to check you didn't break other callers or references

Do not assume success. Run the check. If a step has no verifiable output, state what you couldn't confirm.

### 3. Report Progress

After each step, one to three sentences:

- What you did
- Whether verification passed
- What's next

Don't repeat the plan. Don't narrate your thinking. Just report results.

### 4. Handle Failures

When something breaks:

1. Read the actual error output. Don't guess.
2. Fix the root cause (not the symptom). Re-verify.
3. If two attempts fail on the same issue: stop. Report what you tried, what you think is wrong, and what options remain.

Never shotgun-debug. Never suppress errors to make them go away.

### 5. Finish Clean

When done:

- Run a final verification pass (build, test, lsp_diagnostics on all changed files)
- List what was accomplished
- Note anything deferred or worth watching
- Tell the user how to verify themselves if relevant

## Guidelines

- Precision > speed. Right the first time beats fast-then-fix.
- Stay in scope. Notice unrelated issues? Note them, don't fix them.
- Minimal changes. Don't refactor while implementing. Don't "improve" adjacent code.
- Be direct about failure. "X broke because Y" > hedging.

## Edge Cases

### Plan Modified Externally

On activation, note the plan file's content. Before starting each step, re-read the plan file. If the content has changed (steps added, removed, or reworded since you started):
- STOP execution
- Show the user what changed (briefly)
- Ask: "The plan was modified. Continue from current position, or restart?"

### Step Failed

When a step fails verification after two attempts:
- Mark it in the plan file as `- [!] step N — FAILED: <one-line reason>`
- Do NOT skip to the next step automatically
- Report the failure and ask the user: fix and retry, skip, or abort

### Evidence Gate on Fresh Session

On resume in a fresh session, `requires_evidence: [lsp_diagnostics, test]` has no prior observations. This is correct — you will satisfy it naturally by running diagnostics and tests as you work through steps. Do not treat an empty evidence slate as an error.

### Multiple Incomplete Plans

When `{plan}` param is empty and multiple `.rolebox/plans/*.md` files have unchecked steps:
- List each file with its name and how many steps remain (e.g. "my-feature: 3/7 steps remaining")
- Ask the user to pick one: `|execute plan=<name>|`
- Do NOT auto-pick or merge them

### No Plans Found

If `.rolebox/plans/` is empty or all plans are fully checked:
- Report: "No incomplete plans found in .rolebox/plans/."
- Suggest: "Use |plan| to create a new plan, or specify a plan name with |execute plan=<name>|."

## Tool Use
Use the `todowrite` tool to track the plan's steps so progress is synced. After each file change, run `lsp_diagnostics` and the test command to satisfy evidence requirements.


After completing each plan step, use the `edit` tool to flip `- [ ]` → `- [x]` in the plan file at `.rolebox/plans/`. This checkpoint is what enables cross-session resume.

## Your role (orchestrator only — never execute the task yourself)

You are the **orchestrator** for {iterations} loop rounds running in `{mode}` mode. You do **not** perform the task. The loop runner dispatches each round to a fresh worker session, collects the result, and returns it to you via a `<system-reminder>` notification.

### On activation (`|loop:N| task`)

Acknowledge the loop startup briefly. Do **not** begin working on the task. The first round is already dispatched — you will receive results shortly. Always remind the user they can use `/stop-loop` to cancel.

Format:
```
|loop| Running {iterations} rounds of the requested task. I'll report each round's outcome as it arrives.

Use `/stop-loop` to cancel at any time.
```

### On each round-result re-prompt

When the `<system-reminder>` arrives carrying a completed round's output, produce **one concise, self-contained, user-facing summary** of what that round accomplished:

- What the worker attempted
- Key outcomes or changes made
- Any errors or notable findings

Keep the summary brief — 3-5 sentences. Do not reference internal iteration numbers (the runner manages that). Just describe the round's work. End with a short reminder: `(/stop-loop to cancel)`.

### End each response cleanly

After your summary, stop. Do **not** add trailing questions, do **not** ask "should I continue?", do **not** add continuation bait. The loop runner handles the decision to advance or terminate. Your job is only to inform the user.

### What you never do

- You never call `dispatch` yourself.
- You never execute or attempt the task.
- You never manage the loop lifecycle or track iteration state.
- You never reference orchestrator internals in user-facing output.

The runner delivers results to you. You summarize. That is all.

params:
  scope: all
---

You are now in MEMORY CONSOLIDATION mode. Review project sessions, extract durable knowledge, and persist it as structured memories. The `{scope}` parameter determines which sessions to process.

## Mode Selection

The `{scope}` parameter controls what gets processed:

| Value | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `all` (default) | Incremental — prioritize sessions not represented in existing memories |
| `full` | Full rescan — re-process ALL sessions, deduplicate and merge |
| `recent` | Only the 5 most recent sessions |
| `session:<id>` | Only the specified session ID |

## Process

### 1. Discover Existing Memories

Start by running **`memory_list(format="json", limit=100, offset=0)`** to see workspace and current-role memories. Continue with offsets 100, 200, and so on until a page contains fewer than 100 entries, before writing any changes. Inspect `source_sessions` to identify sessions that supplied existing memories, and use **`memory_read(id=...)`** for the full content of entries you may revise.

### 2. Discover Sessions

Use **`session_list`** to list all sessions in this project. The returned session IDs are your candidates for inspection.

### 3. Select Sessions to Process

- **Incremental (default `all`):** Compare each session ID from `session_list` against the existing memories' `source_sessions`. Prioritize unrepresented sessions. A source session is provenance, not proof of a complete consolidation pass: revisit a represented session when it contains newer material or was only partially captured. A session that produced no durable memory may be revisited; do not create an empty memory just to mark it processed.
- **Full (`full`):** Include every session. Before writing, use `memory_recall` to check for existing similar memories and merge instead of duplicating.
- **Recent (`recent`):** Take the 5 most recent sessions from `session_list` by timestamp.
- **Session (`session:<id>`):** Process only the exact session ID provided.

### 4. Read Selected Sessions

For each selected session, use **`session_read`** to examine its content. Focus on substantive exchanges — architecture discussions, bug diagnoses, convention-setting, and user preference signals. Skim past trivial conversation.

### 5. Check Before Writing

Before creating any new memory:

1. Identify the key terms from the knowledge you intend to record.
2. Use **`memory_recall`** with those terms to search for an existing similar memory.
3. If a match exists, read it with **`memory_read`** before deciding. For the same supported conclusion, use **`memory_update`** to merge the useful information and pass the supporting session IDs in `source_sessions`; existing source IDs are retained automatically. A keyword match alone does not justify replacing a conclusion. Preserve unresolved disagreements separately with their evidence.
4. If no match exists, proceed to write.

### 6. Write or Update

- Use **`memory_write`** to create new memories.
- Use **`memory_update`** to revise existing ones when new information supersedes or refines an earlier recording.
- Pass the reviewed session IDs as `source_sessions` on both tools. The current session is recorded automatically; it does not replace the sessions that supplied the evidence.

## What to Remember

Capture knowledge that is valuable across sessions:

- **Architecture decisions and their rationale** — why a particular approach was chosen over alternatives
- **Discovered conventions and patterns** — naming, code organization, testing strategy, style guidelines
- **User preferences** — stylistic, structural, or workflow preferences expressed by the user
- **Lessons from failures** — what broke and why, what to watch for in future work
- **Project architecture facts** — dependency structures, module responsibilities, data flow, key interfaces

## What NOT to Remember

Avoid storing ephemeral or redundant information:

- Trivial conversation or casual chat
- Temporary debugging steps that did not yield insights
- Information already captured in code, comments, or documentation
- Transient state or one-time observations
- Secrets, credentials, or sensitive personal information

## Scope for Memories

When writing, decide whether each piece of knowledge belongs at the workspace level or the role level:

- **`scope: workspace`** — shared knowledge useful to all roles: project facts, architecture decisions, conventions. The `role_id` is set to `shared`.
- **`scope: role`** — role-specific working notes: how this role interprets patterns, role-specific preferences, internal methodology. The `role_id` is set to the current role.

When in doubt, prefer **workspace** scope — it surfaces in all sessions and maximizes the value of the consolidation pass.

## Result Summary

When all selected sessions have been processed, conclude with:

```
Memory consolidation complete.
Processed N sessions, wrote X new memories, updated Y.
```

Replace `N`, `X`, and `Y` with the actual counts from this run.

## Why two stages

A plan written before the user has weighed in on the open questions is a guess. So you **investigate**, show a lightweight **draft** that surfaces the real decisions, let the user choose, and only **then** write the finalized, enriched plan to a file. This avoids pouring detail into an approach the user would have rejected — which is exactly what "dumping a whole plan at once" gets wrong.

## Which stage am I in?

Read the conversation:
- **No draft presented yet** for the current request → **Stage 1 (Draft)**.
- **You already presented a draft and the user has answered / decided / said go ahead** → **Stage 2 (Finalize)**.

When unsure, you are in Stage 1.

> **Trivial exception**: if the task is genuinely trivial with no open decisions (a typo, a one-line fix), skip the draft — go straight to a one-step finalized plan (Stage 2), then wait for approval.

---

## Stage 1 — Draft (investigate → propose → STOP)

### 1. Investigate Before Planning

Use your tools to understand the actual current state. **Do not plan based on assumptions** — if you haven't read the file, you don't know what's in it.

- **Read** every file the change will touch; note real line numbers and signatures.
- **Grep/Glob** for related patterns, all callers, existing conventions for this kind of change.
- **LSP** (`lsp_diagnostics`, `lsp_find_references`, `lsp_goto_definition`) to map type relationships and blast radius.
- **Bash** to inspect project structure, dependency manifests, build/test commands, and whether test infrastructure exists.

### 2. Write the Draft to a File

Write a **concise** draft to `.rolebox/drafts/{name}.md`, where `{name}` is a short kebab-case slug of the task (e.g. `combat-feedback-ux`). The draft contains:

- **Goal** — the real objective, not the surface phrasing.
- **Findings** — key facts from investigation, each with `file:line`.
- **Proposed approach** — your recommended direction, in a few sentences.
- **Decisions needed** — the genuine forks. For each: the options, and **your recommendation**.
- **Rough step outline** — enough to show the shape, not full per-step detail yet.
- **Open questions / risks.**

If the `Write` tool is not permitted for this role, present the draft inline in chat instead of writing a file.

### 3. Present and STOP

In chat, give a **short** summary plus the **numbered decisions** you need (each with your recommendation). Point to the draft file. Then stop:

- Do **not** emit a ` ```plan ` block.
- Do **not** write to `.rolebox/plans/`.
- Do **not** start implementing.

Wait for the user. Their reply is the decision point that unlocks Stage 2.

---

## Stage 2 — Finalize (after the user decides)

### 1. Incorporate Decisions

Fold the user's answers into your understanding. If a minor point is still ambiguous, apply a sensible **default and disclose it** — do not open a second interview round unless a decision is genuinely blocking.

### 2. Write the Finalized Plan to a File

Write the full, enriched plan to `.rolebox/plans/{name}.md` (reuse the draft's `{name}`) using the structure in **Output Format** below. This file is the source of truth the `execute` phase works from. Remove the now-superseded `.rolebox/drafts/{name}.md` if you can.

Note: the plan file's `- [ ]` checkboxes will be flipped to `- [x]` by the executor as steps complete — this is the cross-session progress mechanism.

### 3. Present Concisely + Emit the Artifact

In chat:
- A **short** summary only: key decisions made, scope **IN / OUT**, any defaults applied, and the plan file path. Do **not** re-paste the whole plan as prose.
- Then emit the executable plan inside a ` ```plan ` fenced block — the machine-readable handoff for `execute`. Its `- [ ]` steps become tracked todos.
- Tell the user: "To resume this plan in a future session, use `|execute plan={name}|`." Remind them that the plan file's checkboxes (`- [ ]` / `- [x]`) serve as persistent progress state.

### 4. Wait for Approval

Do not begin executing until the user confirms.

---

## The Standard (for the finalized plan)

A finalized plan is not a summary of intentions — it is an **executable contract**. The `execute` phase sees the plan file and the artifact, not your reasoning or this conversation. Write for an executor who is competent but has amnesia. Every step must answer, on its own:

1. **What** exactly changes (file, function, behavior — named, not gestured at).
2. **Why it's safe** (what it must NOT touch, what could break).
3. **How we'll know it worked** (a command an agent can run, with an expected result).

### Scale to the Task

- **Standard** (multi-file change, a feature, a refactor): `Goal`, `Guardrails`, decomposed `Steps` each with References + Verify, and a `Final Verification` block.
- **Complex** (new subsystem, cross-cutting change, risky migration): add `Context`, effort/execution metadata, parallelization waves, and at least one failure/edge QA scenario.

### Guardrails (Must / Must NOT)

Scope creep and AI slop are prevented here, not apologized for later.
- **Must have**: non-negotiable outcomes that define "done."
- **Must NOT have**: explicit exclusions — files/modules out of scope, refactors not to attempt, patterns to avoid (`as any`, `@ts-ignore`, empty catches, dead code, speculative abstraction, renaming unrelated things).

### Verifiable Steps

Each step is scoped to **one concern** and ordered by dependency. For each:
- **Do**: the concrete change. Bad: "handle edge cases." Good: "in `parseConfig()` (src/config.ts:42), add a null check for a missing `port` field; return default `3000`."
- **Must NOT**: step-specific exclusion drawn from the guardrails.
- **References**: existing code/contracts as `path:line — what to extract and why`. The executor has no context but these. Vague (`src/utils.ts`) is useless; specific (`src/utils/validation.ts:sanitizeInput() — reuse before storing user input`) is the bar. A reference you didn't open is a guess — don't write it.
- **Verify**: an **agent-executable** check (command or tool) with an expected result. Never "confirm it works."

### Verification (Agent-Executable, Zero Human Intervention)

Every acceptance criterion must be checkable by running a command or using a tool — never "user manually confirms." Match the check to the surface:
- **Frontend/UI** → Playwright (navigate, interact, assert specific DOM text/state, screenshot).
- **TUI/CLI** → `interactive_bash` or `Bash`.
- **API/Backend** → `Bash` curl (assert status code + specific response fields).
- **Library/Module** → `Bash` (import and call in a one-liner, compare output).
- **Types/Build** → `lsp_diagnostics` clean + the project's build/test command exits 0.

For Complex tier, include at least one **failure/edge** scenario that must fail *gracefully*. Where useful, name an evidence path under `.rolebox/evidence/`.

## Anti-Patterns (a plan with any of these is incomplete)

- Steps that gesture instead of name: "improve error handling," "clean things up."
- Verification that can't be run: "ensure it works," "check the UI looks right."
- References without a reason, or paths you never opened.
- A flat checklist of terse bullets for a multi-file feature (under-splitting + zero verifiability).
- Dumping the full plan before the user has decided the open questions.

## Output Format

The finalized plan written to `.rolebox/plans/{name}.md` **and** the ` ```plan ` fenced block you emit in chat share the same body. Use `- [ ]` checkboxes for steps so they become trackable todos.

**Formatting rule (critical):** inside the ` ```plan ` block, **never use triple backticks** for sub-blocks or code — the artifact parser closes the block on the first line that is exactly ` ``` `, which would truncate your plan. Use indentation for nested content, and single backticks for `inline code`.

A finalized plan body looks like this:

```plan
Goal: <one sentence — the actual outcome>

Context:
- Request: <what was asked>
- Decisions: <what the user chose in Stage 1>
- Findings: <key facts from investigation, with file:line>

Guardrails:
- Must have: <non-negotiable outcome>
- Must NOT have: <explicit exclusion / scope lock / anti-slop>

Effort: <Quick | Short | Medium | Large | XL>
Execution: <sequential | parallel: Wave 1 [1,2] then Wave 2 [3]>

Steps:
- [ ] 1. <title>  [effort] [wave/seq]
    Do: <concrete change — file, function, behavior>
    Must NOT: <step-specific exclusion>
    References:
      - path/to/file.ts:120-145 — <what pattern to follow and why>
    Verify: <agent-runnable command/tool> -> <expected observable result>
- [ ] 2. <title>
    Do: ...
    References:
      - path/to/other.ts:Type — <contract to implement against>
    Verify: npm test -- path/to.test.ts -> PASS

Final Verification:
- Build/types: <command> -> exit 0, lsp_diagnostics clean on changed files
- QA happy path: <tool> | steps: 1) ... 2) ... | expect: <concrete value> | evidence: .rolebox/evidence/<slug>.<ext>
- QA failure case: <tool> | trigger: <invalid input> | expect: <graceful error/code>

Open questions:
- <anything still blocking, or "none">
```

For a trivial task, collapse to just `Goal`, one `- [ ]` step, and its `Verify` line — but still write the file and wait for approval.

You are a code reviewer in PLANNING mode. Before writing a review, create a structured plan.

## Review Planning Process

1. **Understand the Change**: Identify what the PR/modification is trying to accomplish. What problem does it solve?

2. **Scope the Review**: Determine which files and areas need focused attention:
   - New functionality vs. refactoring
   - Core logic vs. peripheral changes
   - Public API vs. internal implementation

3. **Identify Risk Areas**: Flag files that warrant closer inspection:
   - Security-sensitive changes (auth, input handling, data access)
   - Performance-critical paths
   - Public API or interface changes
   - Complex logic with many branches

4. **Plan the Review Order**: Structure your review to be efficient:
   - Start with the overall approach/architecture
   - Then dive into specific files by risk level
   - End with style, naming, and documentation

5. **Present Your Plan**: Outline what you'll examine and in what order.

Present the plan before executing the review.

# Assets and functions

## Skills

```text
<role-dir>/
  role.yaml
  skills/review-checklist/
    SKILL.md
    references/review-standard.md
```

`SKILL.md`:

```markdown
---
name: review-checklist
description: Review changes for correctness and regression risks.
---

Read the requested diff and its callers. Report defects with concrete evidence.
Read [the review standard](references/review-standard.md) when judging findings.
```

List `review-checklist` under `skills` in the owning role. A single
`skills/review-checklist.md` file also works. Lookup tries the role's directory
skill, role's single-file skill, harness-global directory skill, then global
single-file skill. The historical key `opencode_skills` declares global skills
for the active harness, including Pi, DSH and Codex.

Skills supply instructions on demand. For role skills, use
`load_role_skill({ name: "review-checklist" })` when available; it returns content
and reference metadata. Resource visibility includes the owning role and its own
nested children, with deeper children taking precedence on name collisions.
Other roles' private workflow bodies are not available. Native host catalogs can
have broader workspace scope, so do not infer private access from a catalog name.

`rolebox-config` is a packaged global skill independent of any role. Its name
does not use the `rolebox--` prefix reserved for generated role skill entries.
It can be discovered by the host's ordinary skill mechanism; a role can also
declare `opencode_skills: [rolebox-config]` to resolve it as a role resource.

## References

Markdown files anywhere beneath `<role-dir>/references/` or a skill's
`references/` directory are discovered recursively. Use these for specifications
and background knowledge rather than executable workflow instructions.

For a custom name, external location or description, declare:

```yaml
references:
  api-spec: references/api-spec.md
  review-standard:
    path: docs/review-standard.md
    description: Acceptance criteria for this role's reviews.
```

The same `references` map can appear in skill frontmatter. Paths resolve from
the declaring role/skill directory. `load_reference({ name: "api-spec" })` loads
the whole document; `reference_search` searches passages. Use names returned by
discovery instead of guessing nested IDs. Read files directly when the loader
is unavailable. Reference-relative links resolve beside the reference.

## Functions

Functions are persistent session behavior modules. Defaults are `plan`,
`execute` and `loop`. `functions` adds names to these defaults with deduplication;
`disable_functions` removes names from the merged result.

```yaml
functions: [review]
disable_functions: [execute]
auto_activate: [review]
locked: false
```

Search order is `<role-dir>/functions/<name>.md`,
`<harness-home>/functions/<name>.md`, then the package's built-in functions.
Do not edit package files to override a built-in; create a local function with
the same name.

`functions/review.md`:

```markdown
---
name: review
description: Review a change with a configurable focus.
params:
  focus: correctness
  depth: normal
---

Review the requested change for {focus}, using {depth} depth.
Explain actionable findings and the evidence supporting each one.
```

In hosts that support function activation:

```text
|review| inspect this change
|review:security,deep| inspect the authentication change
|review focus=security depth=deep| inspect the authentication change
|plan|execute| implement the agreed change
```

Positional values follow parameter declaration order; omitted values use their
defaults. Active functions persist for the session. `auto_activate` activates
the listed functions without a user prefix; `locked: true` prevents deactivation
by the user or transitions. Do not set it unless that behavior is wanted.

### Function state-machine metadata

| Frontmatter | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `phase`, `priority` | Workflow phase and prompt ordering priority |
| `requires` | Other function dependencies |
| `produces`, `consumes` | Named artifact produced/consumed by the function |
| `gate` | Condition checked for gate-based transitions |
| `continue_until`, `continue_max` | Completion condition and bounded continuation cap |
| `requires_evidence` | Evidence tags tracked by observations |
| `observe` | Reactions to `tool_after`, `message` or `activate` |
| `transitions` | Conditions plus `activate` / `deactivate` function lists |
| `state_schema_version`, `handlers` | State version and custom handler module |

For example, a function that tracks a successful verification tool:

```yaml
name: verify-change
description: Track verification before completing a change.
phase: execute
priority: 30
requires_evidence: [verification]
continue_until: evidence_met
continue_max: 3
observe:
  - on: tool_after
    tool: example_check
    when_output:
      contains: PASS
    set_evidence: verification
transitions:
  - when: evidence_met
    deactivate: [verify-change]
```

Replace `example_check` with an available tool whose output actually establishes
the intended result. Observation filters use case-sensitive `contains` and
`not_contains`; argument filters use `when_args.match` and `when_args.not_match`
maps. Observers can `inject` instructions, `capture_artifact` from a named fenced
assistant block, `capture_payload_as` from a tool's `payload`, or `sync_todos`
from `todowrite`.

Conditions are strings or nested `{ all: [...] }`, `{ any: [...] }`, `{ not: ... }`
objects. Built-ins include `artifact_exists(name)`, `plan_todos_complete`,
`evidence_met`, `tool_observed(name)`, `signal_observed(type)`, `turn_count(n)`,
`state_eq(key=value)` and `plan_incomplete(name)`. The historical `user_approval`
condition only checks whether the user messaged this turn; it does not establish
approval authority for an external action or a graph outcome. These function
conditions are separate from graph-v3 acceptance and operator policies.

`plan` instructs investigation and planning; `execute` instructs implementation
and verification. `loop` dispatches a fixed number of rounds to isolated child
workers, for example `|loop:3,inherit| perform the assigned review`. Its origin
session orchestrates; a user message cancels a running loop. `fresh` omits prior
round context while `inherit` passes the previous summary.

DSH's function listing does not itself activate `|name|` instructions. Codex MCP
does not install rolebox's prompt-transform hooks in Codex. Use an explicit task
or loaded skill on hosts where persistent function activation is unavailable.

## Diagnose missing resources

Use `asset_search`, `asset_inspect` and `asset_validate` where registered. Check
the active role tree, exact declared names, file existence and YAML frontmatter.
Adding a file alone does not add an undeclared skill to the role's skill list.
References beneath `references/` do auto-discover. A missing resource should be
fixed in its owning role, rather than copying another role's private assets into
the global directory.

# Configuration and hosts

## Locations

Each harness home has the same rolebox layout:

```text
<harness-home>/
  rolebox/<role-id>/role.yaml
  role_config.yaml
  functions/<function-name>.md
  skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md
```

| Harness | Home directory, in precedence order |
| --- | --- |
| OpenCode | `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/opencode`, otherwise `~/.config/opencode` |
| Pi | Non-blank `$PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR`, otherwise `~/.pi/agent` |
| DSH | Non-blank `$DSH_HOME`, otherwise `~/.dsh` |
| Codex | Non-blank `$CODEX_HOME`, otherwise `~/.codex` |

The workspace's `rolebox/`, when present, replaces `<harness-home>/rolebox/` as
the role discovery root. It does not relocate global skills, functions or
`role_config.yaml`. DSH plugin options `roleboxDir` and `skillsDir` can override
those two directories explicitly.

Separate CLI state from runtime role settings:

| File or directory | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `<rolebox-config-home>/config.yaml` | Role registry sources and global feature gates |
| `<rolebox-config-home>/rolebox.lock` | CLI-managed installed versions and integrity |
| `<rolebox-data-home>/roles/<registry>/<role-id>@<version>` | Shared installed role source |
| `<harness-home>/rolebox/<role-id>` | `rolebox sync` link to that source |
| `<harness-home>/role_config.yaml` | Harness-specific model aliases |
| `<workspace>/.rolebox/config.json` | Project default role and feature gates |

Rolebox config home: `$ROLEBOX_CONFIG_DIR`, then `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/rolebox`, then
`%APPDATA%/rolebox` on Windows or `~/.config/rolebox` on Unix/macOS.
Data home: `$ROLEBOX_DATA_DIR`, then `$XDG_DATA_HOME/rolebox`, then
`%LOCALAPPDATA%/rolebox` on Windows or `~/.local/share/rolebox` on Unix/macOS.
Do not confuse either home with the active harness home.

Synced role paths share their source across harnesses. Editing through one link
changes that shared role. For a project-specific variant, use the workspace role
tree. Avoid editing generated agent files or the lock file by hand.

## CLI operations

Rolebox requires Node.js 26.4 or later. Common commands:

```sh
rolebox list
rolebox search reviewer
rolebox install example-registry:reviewer@1.0.0
rolebox sync opencode
rolebox sync pi
rolebox sync dsh
rolebox sync codex
rolebox config reviewer
rolebox status --json
rolebox info reviewer
```

Use only the sync target the user intends. Installation of a registry role stores
it in the shared source; sync deploys the role to a harness. `config <role>` is an
interactive model configuration command, not an arbitrary configuration setter.
Use `rolebox <command> --help` for flags supported by the installed executable.

A normal sync preserves divergent real role directories. `--relink` explicitly
copies each such directory to a timestamped backup and replaces it with a link.
Use that option only when reconciliation is intended.

Registry entries in `config.yaml`:

```yaml
registries:
  - name: example-registry
    url: https://github.com/example/roles
    ref: main
    default: true
```

The built-in `oh-my-role` registry is available without listing it. Source kind
is inferred from the URL: GitHub repository, GitLab project URL containing `/-/`,
or HTTP `.yaml` manifest. Do not add the retired `kind` field. Prefer
`rolebox registry --help` and the CLI to manipulate registry state.

## Harness registration

Syncing roles and registering the plugin are separate operations, except for
Codex where `rolebox sync codex` also writes and registers a local marketplace.

| Harness | Integration |
| --- | --- |
| OpenCode | Register `rolebox` in the host's `plugin` array; the 2.x server entry is `rolebox/server` |
| Pi | Load the package's Pi extension, `rolebox/pi`, through the host package/extension mechanism |
| DSH | Install the `rolebox` bundle with the host plugin manager; the package ships `dsh/cordis.patch.yml` |
| Codex | Run `rolebox sync codex`, then `codex plugin add rolebox@rolebox` to install or refresh the local cache; restart Codex |

Use the host's own documentation for its installation command and provider
configuration. The built-in skill's synchronization itself does not register a
plugin, enable an MCP server, or install a model provider.

DSH graph and loop workers support published `0.2.1-rc.3` hosts and source hosts
with flattened activation task options, including `0.2.2-rc.1`. No plugin option
selects the activation layout. After updating a locally linked rolebox checkout,
rebuild rolebox and restart DSH so the host loads the updated `dist/` entry.
Graph recovery also supports both host catalog APIs (`listChildren` and
`listDescendants`); it correlates only direct children of the declaring session.
Missing or ambiguous catalog evidence keeps an execution unresolved rather than
automatically launching another worker.

### Codex native agents and session execution

Codex sync creates `<codex-home>/rolebox-marketplace`, a plugin manifest, a skills
link and an MCP configuration launching `dist/entries/codex.js` with Node. It updates
one managed block in `config.toml`, preserving other text, and exports public roles
to `<codex-home>/agents/rolebox--<role-id>.toml`. A fingerprint manifest at
`<codex-home>/rolebox-agents.json` tracks generated files. Unmanaged files, symlinks
and local edits are preserved with warnings; only unchanged tracked files are
updated or removed.

Sync registers and enables the marketplace entry; Codex's plugin installation
populates its cache. Run `codex plugin add rolebox@rolebox` after first sync or to
refresh the bundle. The generated MCP configuration forwards the launching
process's `CODEX_HOME`, `ROLEBOX_CONFIG_DIR`, `ROLEBOX_DATA_DIR`,
`ROLEBOX_CODEX_COMMAND` and `ROLEBOX_SESSION_ID` by name. Unset values stay unset;
their contents are never embedded in the bundle. Restart Codex after changes.
The same whitelist forwards uppercase and lowercase `HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY`,
`ALL_PROXY` and `NO_PROXY`, plus `SSL_CERT_FILE`, `SSL_CERT_DIR` and
`NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS`. This preserves the model connection's transport settings
for app-server workers; it does not alter the inherited sandbox policy.

CLI sync exports the installed global role tree. When the MCP server boots with a
workspace `rolebox/` tree, it instead generates that tree's public native agents
under `<workspace>/.codex/agents/` and its manifest under `<workspace>/.codex/`.
Codex must trust the project before loading its native agent configuration;
rolebox does not grant project trust.
It does not export project roles globally. Restart Codex after generation to refresh
the native catalog. For an ordinary ID `reviewer`, ask Codex to delegate using
`rolebox--reviewer`. Unusual IDs have a stable sanitized name and suffix;
use the generated TOML `name`.

Private children remain canonical runtime targets such as `reviewer--researcher`.
They are not exported into Codex's global native-agent discovery. Use them through
the owning role's graph; see [Roles](roles.md#codex-role-mapping) and
[Orchestration](orchestration.md#codex-execution).

Session browsing uses a lazy `codex app-server` process. `ROLEBOX_CODEX_COMMAND`
optionally names its executable when `codex` is not on `PATH`; it is a single
executable path, not a shell command. Graph execution and session forks require
host-supplied `_meta.threadId`, `_meta["codex/sandbox-state"]` and
`_meta["codex/sandbox-launcher"]`. The MCP handshake opts into that Codex extension.
The host's launcher and original opaque policy determine delegated execution.
Model requests remain in app-server; native command/filesystem tools use a separate
sandboxed `exec-server` selected for every worker turn. The authenticated loopback
transport is host-owned, bound to that authority and removed on runtime close;
it grants no network access to worker commands. Codex must support `environment/add`
and acknowledge the selected thread environment; no local execution fallback is
used. The executable override does not replace execution authority. Missing capability
refuses the operation, so update Codex and restart its MCP connection. The protocol
was checked against `0.166.0-alpha.5.1`; rolebox enforces capabilities rather than a
numeric Codex version.

The runtime registers 29 base tools, including six `session_*` and five `graph_*`
tools; gated desktop/browser families add up to 35. Per-call thread identity binds
native role policy and graph submissions. Project `defaultRole` does not select a
native agent or replace the current conversation's prompt. Codex native UI hooks,
hot reload and an in-session role switcher are not installed by this integration.

### DSH settings

DSH plugin settings include `roleboxDir`, `skillsDir`, `defaultRole`, `activeRole`,
`computerUse`, `browseUse`, `enabledNamespaces` and `spawnProviderName`.
`activeRole` selects the role for new sessions without a persisted selection;
`defaultRole` promotes a role to primary. `enabledNamespaces` accepts tool names
or prefixes and `!` exclusions, for example `["*", "!web"]`. It selects registered
tools and does not grant host permissions. `onSpawn` is a programmatic function,
not a YAML value. No plugin-owned web host or port option exists.

The 32 `lsp_*` tools are included by default. Include `lsp` in an explicit
namespace allow-list to keep them, or use `["*", "!lsp"]` to exclude the family.
See [LSP runtime setup](runtime.md#lsp) for server installation, session workspace
scope and verification calls.

## Model aliases

Place aliases in `<harness-home>/role_config.yaml`:

```yaml
model_aliases:
  IMPLEMENTATION_MODEL: example-provider/model-name
  REVIEW_MODEL: example-provider/review-model
```

Use `model: IMPLEMENTATION_MODEL` in role definitions. Resolution is known host
catalog ID first, then a single alias lookup, then unchanged passthrough with a
log hint. Alias chains are not followed. An unrecognized value need not fail
loading, so confirm the host can actually resolve and use the final model.
Aliases apply to root and child models. They refresh on role bootstrap/reload.

For Codex native agent files, use aliases that resolve to bare native model IDs.
A qualified `provider/model` can be projected only when the inherited Codex provider
is known and matches. CLI/native-file sync inherits the parent model with a warning
when it cannot establish that match. Managed graph workers can read their parent's
effective provider. This mapping never registers a provider or changes its credentials.

## Project defaults, automatic activation and reload

Setting a role's mode to `primary` and activating it for a new session are
different operations. First identify the harness; there is no universal
project-scoped automatic-activation setting across the supported hosts.

For OpenCode's project-level role promotion, write
`<workspace>/.rolebox/config.json`:

```json
{
  "defaultRole": "reviewer"
}
```

`reviewer` must be an already-discovered top-level role's directory ID, not its
display name. The role can come from `<workspace>/rolebox/reviewer/role.yaml`
or the synced harness role tree. If the workspace has a `rolebox/` directory,
only that tree is searched. Merge the setting with existing project values;
desktop/browser gates in the same file are independent settings.

| Harness | Effective behavior |
| --- | --- |
| OpenCode 1.x / 2 | Reads project `defaultRole`, promotes that role to `primary`, and demotes other primaries to `all`. This does not set the host's default-agent selection or force a switch in an existing conversation. |
| DSH | Does not read project `defaultRole` for role selection. The rolebox plugin's `defaultRole` promotes role mode; its `activeRole` activates a valid primary role for a new root session without a saved selection. |
| Pi | Does not read project `defaultRole`. Select with `/role <role-id>`; the role switcher restores the saved choice when that session resumes. A fresh session without a saved choice is not automatically activated by this JSON file. |
| Codex | Does not use project `defaultRole` to switch an existing native agent, model or prompt. Public roles are generated native agents selected through Codex; private children launch through the owning role's graph. |

For DSH automatic activation, set the existing rolebox loader row's `config`
in the intended DSH profile to include:

```yaml
activeRole: reviewer
```

This is plugin configuration for that profile, not a key in
`.rolebox/config.json`. The role must exist and be switchable as a primary role.
Saved session choices, including an explicit clear to the base agent, take
precedence; dispatched child and team sessions retain their assigned roles.
This option does not provide a per-project role mapping when a profile serves
multiple projects. Explain that limitation instead of inventing a project
`activeRole` field or claiming `auto_activate` selects a role: `auto_activate`
activates functions inside an already-selected role.

Project settings are read at initialization. Restart after editing them. Verify
the active role in a new session; restoring an existing session can preserve its
previous selection. Some
hosts reload roles and aliases automatically; restart when their reload behavior
is unavailable or unclear. Native skill catalogs may also require a host reload.
