# Orchestration

## Choose the available execution mechanism

Private subagents belong to a role and execute assigned work using their own
prompt/model/assets. Direct dispatch is useful for one task; declared graphs
express fixed dependencies, outcomes, joins and bounded revision cycles. DSH
role teams coordinate complementary top-level roles in persistent sessions.

Use the tools actually registered by the current host. Codex supplies the graph
surface through its managed app-server workers; its native public-agent discovery
and private rolebox graph targets have different scopes. See
[Codex execution](#codex-execution) before configuring that host.

## Direct dispatch settings

The effective role-level YAML settings are positive numbers in milliseconds:

```yaml
dispatch:
  backgroundStaleTimeoutMs: 900000
  syncPromptTimeoutMs: 600000
```

Supported global environment overrides include:

| Variable | Meaning and default |
| --- | --- |
| `ROLEBOX_DISPATCH_BG_STALE_MS` | Background stale timeout; 900000 |
| `ROLEBOX_DISPATCH_MATERIALIZE_TIMEOUT_MS` | Result fetch timeout; 10000 |
| `ROLEBOX_DISPATCH_RESULT_RETENTION_MS` | Result retention; 3600000 |

Environment values take precedence over role settings and defaults. Do not put
`maxInputTokensPerRequest`, `maxCostPerRequest` or similar budget fields in the
`dispatch` block: the current YAML loader retains only the two timeout fields.
Do not assume an environment variable exists just because a manager type has a
similarly named field. Use graph budgets for declared graph execution limits.

Where available, `dispatch` accepts the resolved subagent ID and prompt;
background dispatch returns a task ID, `dispatch_output` retrieves its result
and `dispatch_cancel` cancels it. Reusing `session_id` continues a prior worker
session. Wait for completion notifications before collecting results. Read the
registered schema for background flags and per-task `timeout_ms` support.

## Graph engine v3

The effective interface declares a complete version-3 document through
`graph_declare`, starts/controls it through `graph_control`, and reads
`graph_status`/`graph_audit`. Workers submit a declared outcome through their
dedicated `graph_submit_outcome` entry point. Read actual tool schemas for the
transport wrapper around the declaration and control commands.

`graph_status` omits node prompt bodies by default, including in run history.
Use `include_prompt: true` when you need the full node instructions. Text search
still matches stored prompts when they are omitted from the result; this option
does not change the declaration, worker delivery or audit records.

There are no incremental `graph_create` / `graph_add_node` / `graph_add_edge`
construction tools in this protocol. Signals do not settle graph-v3 nodes.
`graph: { orchestration: graph_v2 }` in `role.yaml` is recognized legacy metadata
with no runtime effect, and is not how to configure a runnable v3 workflow.

A minimal declaration (replace the agent ID with a resolved, visible role):

```json
{
  "version": 3,
  "name": "review-flow",
  "budget": { "max_executions": 4 },
  "nodes": [
    {
      "id": "review",
      "agent": "reviewer--researcher",
      "prompt": "Review the assigned change and submit the done outcome with findings.",
      "completion": { "mode": "explicit" },
      "budget": { "timeout_ms": 600000 },
      "outcomes": [{ "id": "done" }]
    }
  ],
  "edges": []
}
```

The graph's name is its ID. Nodes declare unique IDs, an `agent`, a `prompt` and
one or more outcomes. Edges use `{ "from": "work", "to": "review",
"outcome": "done" }`: the outcome must be declared by the source node.
An outcome may declare `data: { schema, version? }` and ordered
`acceptance: [{ validator, version? }]` requirements. Requested validators must
be installed by the host at that exact identity.

Consumers can declare `inputs: [{ from: "work", outcome: "done" }]` to receive
accepted upstream results. Fan-in uses `join: { strategy: "all" }`, `any`, or
`quorum` plus a positive `quorum` number. A loop group declares `id`, member
`nodes`, positive `max_traversals`, `continuation_outcome` and `exit_outcome`.
Continuation edges stay inside that group; the exit must reach a valid terminal
path. Use explicit outcomes and bounded groups for revision cycles.

Root `budget.max_executions` caps all authorized dispatches in a run, including
loop iterations and new manual retries. Omission declares no ceiling; zero
prevents the first dispatch. Node budgets accept `max_input_tokens`,
`max_output_tokens`, `max_cost_usd` and `timeout_ms` (zero disables that node's
staleness watchdog). `max_retries` is rejected, including zero. Recorded token
usage limits future dispatch and does not cancel work already running.

### Worker tool presentation

Workers inherit the parent's authorized task tools. `tools` on a node is legacy
metadata and does not restrict, grant or register tools. Graph control, team
orchestration and recursive dispatch remain unavailable to workers.

On DSH this includes parent-authorized `lsp_*` tools. Formatting and
`lsp_execute_code_action` can write files and have no separate default LSP write
gate. Use the acting parent role's `tools` policy to deny `lsp_format_document`,
`lsp_format_range` and/or `lsp_execute_code_action` before dispatch; canonical
denials also cover `rb_` aliases. See [LSP runtime setup](runtime.md#lsp) for an
example and workspace lifetime behavior.

Optional `toolPresentation` selects `native` (default), `discover`, or `code`,
with up to 32 exact tool names under `preload`. This changes schema visibility,
not authorization. DSH supports discovery and code invocation. Pi and OpenCode 2
support native discovery but reject code invocation; OpenCode 1 rejects explicit
presentation configuration. Codex supports native presentation only and refuses
`discover` and `code`.
Worker instructions should use available native tools and the dedicated outcome
submission instead of inventing shell or file wrapper APIs.

### Codex execution

Codex registers `graph_declare`, `graph_submit_outcome`, `graph_status`,
`graph_audit` and `graph_control` over the same graph application and acceptance
ledger. Public native agents have names such as `rolebox--reviewer`, while graph
nodes use canonical IDs such as `reviewer` or the acting role's direct private
child `reviewer--researcher`. A base conversation may target public roles only.
Deeper child IDs can be resolved, but graph workers cannot recursively dispatch;
normal Codex workflows therefore do not provide a general launch path for deeper
private descendants.

Graph execution requires Codex to supply trusted per-call `_meta.threadId`, opaque
`codex/sandbox-state` and `codex/sandbox-launcher` metadata. Model arguments cannot
supply that authority. The app-server owns the model connection, while a separate
`codex exec-server` owns native command and filesystem operations. Rolebox launches
that executor through the verified sandbox launcher, forwarding the original
opaque policy unchanged. Thus a network-restricted workspace still permits the
model connection while worker commands retain their network and filesystem limits.
Missing metadata refuses execution.
Worker turns declare `externalSandbox` with restricted network access to avoid
nesting another OS sandbox inside that protected executor. The original policy is
still enforced by the outer launcher and is never replaced by this declaration.

Every worker turn is pinned to this execution environment. An authenticated
loopback relay connects app-server to the executor's stdio; it cannot launch a
command outside that executor. Environment registration or binding failure refuses
execution, and executor loss closes its owning app-server without local fallback
or automatic restart. Codex must support `exec-server`, `environment/add` and
thread/turn environment selection. Forks defer inherited goal continuation; any
later worker turn receives the same mandatory environment binding.
An updated policy gets a separate connection, while existing workers retain their
original policy. [Configuration](configuration.md#codex-native-agents-and-session-execution)
describes installation and executable lookup.

Each attempt runs in a confirmed native thread with its role's prompt, supported
model/effort and feature restrictions. Worker dynamic callbacks are bound to their
connection, thread, turn and graph attempt. The exposed dynamic tools are
`graph_submit_outcome` and allowed role-scoped asset/reference/skill readers.
Native Codex tools perform file and shell work inside the inherited sandbox;
outer-process mutating tools are not exposed through this bridge. Plugins, apps, memories,
MCP servers, recursive native agents, hooks, notifications, hosted web/image tools,
goals and shell snapshots are disabled for these workers. MCP inventory entries
must be explicitly disabled with empty tool/resource catalogs before the worker
model starts; absent or uncertain status is refused. Interactive
approval/input requests are rejected rather than approved automatically.

Only accepted submissions settle explicit outcomes. Normal, failed and interrupted
turns remain distinct; an interrupt acknowledgment is `requested` until the
interrupted terminal event arrives. Cancellation requested while `turn/start` is
pending is queued until its turn ID is known, without claiming interruption.
If a stopping decision arrives during thread creation, the late-created worker
is recorded without starting a model turn. Initialization failure closes the
owning app-server rather than leaving a usable partial connection.
`budget.max_executions` and node `timeout_ms` remain supported. A positive timeout
starts at attempt delivery and includes startup time; the watchdog records a durable
timeout control for that exact attempt and requests interruption. Zero disables the
timeout. Expiry does not retry work automatically or confirm that a turn stopped.
Codex node `max_input_tokens`, `max_output_tokens` and
`max_cost_usd` are refused because this adapter has no measured token/cost feed.

Collect results through `graph_status`, including output/history as needed, and
apply explicit lifecycle changes through `graph_control`. A fresh stdio app-server
cannot wake or automatically resume an external UI-owned conversation. Keep
collecting status while workers run or inspect it in a later turn; do not expect a
completion notification to start the parent agent. Boot does not redispatch
persisted graphs. Fatal transport failure terminates its app-server process tree;
local close and connection loss leave an execution without a native terminal event
unknown, without inventing failure, completion or interruption. Uncertain create
claims are retained; credentials are not retained durably. Diagnose the recorded state before
an explicit retry instead of declaring a duplicate graph to recover it.

On DSH, a model response rejected as `MALFORMED_RESPONSE` specifically because
`graph_submit_outcome` contains invalid JSON gets up to two submission repairs
per worker turn. The host keeps the same session, step and graph attempt, adds
the failed argument draft with its credential redacted to that worker's context,
and asks it to correct the submission without repeating completed work. The
worker must reuse the original handoff credential; acceptance gates still run
normally. These repairs do not create graph executions or consume additional
`max_executions`, but model requests still consume tokens. This is automatic,
with no graph/role setting; restart the DSH plugin to load an updated build.

Recovery requires the host's request-error hook and writable session message
surface, and a diagnostic carrying the failed arguments (at most 131,072 UTF-16
code units). Cancellation, other tool failures, transport errors and output truncation
are not covered. After the repair limit the host's normal error handling applies;
do not assume a failed attempt was accepted. For large reports, keep submissions
concise and reference existing artifacts where the declared contract permits.

### Operator-installed graph policy

These are startup environment variables, not fields that a graph or worker may
install for itself:

| Variable | Trusted configuration |
| --- | --- |
| `ROLEBOX_GRAPH_APPROVAL_POLICY` | JSON `{ id, revision, rules }`; each rule binds `graphId`, `nodeId`, allowed `approverSessions` and optional `mode` |
| `ROLEBOX_GRAPH_COMPLETION_POLICIES` | JSON `{ declare, authorize }`; declaration bodies plus exact authorized `id@revision` identities |
| `ROLEBOX_GRAPH_COMMAND_CHECKS` | JSON array binding `graph`, `node`, `outcome`, `argv`, `cwd`, `timeout_ms`, `expect_exit_code` and non-empty `artifact_refs` |

Approval mode defaults to `independent-review`, which forbids self-approval.
`operator-confirmation` explicitly permits it but supplies no independent review.
Requests pin policy identity/content, target session and an expiry. No installed
policy means no approval authority. Natural completion requests an installed
policy with root `completion_policy: { id, revision }`; an offered body without
authorization is insufficient. Command-exit acceptance needs a trusted binding
for that exact graph/node/outcome. Do not synthesize any of these authorities to
make a failing declaration pass.

Read the audit and results before claiming success. A `stopped` run cannot be
fixed with node-scoped retry; inspect existing effects before an authorized
run-wide retry creates a successor run. Do not delete graph state to bypass a
storage error or reset a budget. A store backup must include its matching
`graph-store.identity`, and restoration requires stopping every holder first.

## Role teams (DSH)

Teams use exact top-level role IDs, not another role's children. The host needs
resumable agents, durable sessions, execution guards and prompt contributions;
team tools register only when these capabilities are present. No `open_roles`
allowlist is required.

Use `team_list_roles`, `team_create`, `team_add`, `team_send_event`, `team_status`,
`team_remove`, `team_delete` and `team_resume` according to their schemas. Adding
a member does not start its turn; an addressed event wakes it. A member must
successfully claim a task before editing shared work, then publish the result
through a team event. Final replies alone remain private. Events are shared
with all members, even when only one recipient is woken. `recipient` names one
active peer by member ID or role ID and an event addressed to its own sender is
rejected, because it would wake nobody; omit `recipient` to wake every other member.

`team_create` returns a compact receipt with the team ID, creator/member
identities, status and turn budget; it does not echo the submitted goal or return
the event history. `team_send_event` returns the event ID, sequence, type, sender,
resolved recipient, task ID (when applicable), timestamp and effective wake flag,
without echoing the submitted content. Full goals and event/task bodies remain
stored and delivered to peers; retrieve them with `team_status(team_id, after_seq?)`
when needed. These receipts do not mean a peer has already finished or even
started its turn. Restart DSH with the updated build to use the new responses.

`team_create` accepts `max_turns` (1–100, default 40); a team has at most eight
members and two in-flight deliveries. Failure pauses the team; resume preserves
the consumed turn budget. The turn cap does not measure tokens or money. Team
execution on OpenCode, Pi and Codex is not implemented by this integration.

Team turns have no elapsed-time execution limit: a role may work for longer
than 15 minutes. The scheduler checks live host activity and session ownership;
it does not require model-generated heartbeat messages or cancel a quiet,
long-running task. A live agent or another live host's session lease keeps an
execution protected. An unfinished persisted turn without a live owner is
interrupted, not evidence that the role is still working. Unknown activity is
not treated as idle or successful completion.

After inspecting errors and existing work, any active member can use `team_resume`
to restore disconnected members in their original sessions, including members
whose failed delivery was already cleared. Restoration retains history, role,
task state and user input. The caller's confirmed current delivery and other
confirmed running deliveries continue; only stopped or ambiguous deliveries
need reconciliation or confirmed cancellation before
pending events are replayed. A failed or discarded delivery releases its turn
reservation, but completed turns remain charged and resume does not reset the
budget. Exhausting the budget prevents new deliveries while already authorized
turns can finish and publish results. Explicit role changes, unavailable models
and another live host's ownership still prevent taking over a member. Session setup, event delivery and
cancellation acknowledgements retain their bounded waits; these are not limits
on how long a role may execute. Restart DSH with the updated build to load this
behavior; no timeout setting or heartbeat configuration is required.
Adding/removing members and deleting a team remain creator-only operations.
Task claim leases remain 30 minutes and can be renewed; an in-flight delivery
protects its member's claims from expiry. This is separate from session liveness.

Removing a member or deleting a team releases its team session descriptor and
lease. Peers created or resumed by rolebox are disposed. When DSH has restored a
peer itself, the host keeps that session and pending user input; rolebox clears
queued team deliveries before releasing the team identity. Cleanup waits while
another running host holds the peer lease, and failed cleanup is retried.

On DSH a peer session is created through the host agent factory, so rolebox
attaches it to the Workspace that owns its directory; this is best effort, and a
host without a Workspace registry leaves peers ungrouped. Peers created by older
builds are repaired when the team's workspace runtime is restored at boot.

On hosts that compose agents through agent presets (the DSH Web profile), rolebox
resolves the host's default agent preset for each peer, records it on the peer
session, and mounts it before the peer's first turn, so a peer starts with the
same capability set as a new conversation. A host without an agent-preset
registry keeps its process-wide composition.

# Roles

## A working role

Create `<role-root>/reviewer/role.yaml`:

```yaml
name: Reviewer
description: Reviews changes for correctness and missing verification.
model: example-provider/model-name
mode: primary
temperature: 0.2
prompt: |
  Review the requested change. Explain actionable defects with evidence.
skills:
  - review-checklist
memory:
  inject: true
  max_inject: 10
  min_relevance: medium
  scope: both
```

Create the declared skill before loading this role; see [Assets](assets.md).
The directory `reviewer` is the ID. Top-level IDs cannot contain the reserved
`--` separator. Give each role a non-empty `name`, a useful `description` and
either `prompt` or `prompt_file`. `prompt_file` is relative to the role directory;
use one prompt source to avoid ambiguity.

## Role fields

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `name`, `description` | Display name and discovery description |
| `prompt` / `prompt_file` | Inline instructions / path to instruction file |
| `version` | Optional role version string |
| `model` | Canonical provider/model string, alias, or inherited host default when absent |
| `mode` | `primary` (default), `subagent` or `all` |
| `color`, `variant` | Host-dependent display/model metadata |
| `temperature`, `top_p` | Model sampling settings; keep within the provider's supported ranges |
| `skills`, `opencode_skills` | Role-local and harness-global skill names |
| `functions`, `disable_functions` | Add to default functions / remove named functions |
| `auto_activate`, `locked` | Automatically activate listed functions / prevent their deactivation |
| `references` | Map of reference names to paths or `{ path, description }` |
| `permission`, `tools` | Role tool policy, subject to host enforcement |
| `memory` | Summary injection and DSH recall settings |
| `subagents` | Inline child definitions; directories also work |
| `dispatch` | Background and synchronous prompt timeouts |
| `hooks`, `copilot` | Lifecycle and continuation behavior |
| `graph` | Legacy selector only; see [Orchestration](orchestration.md) for effective graph configuration |

`open`, `exports` and `open_roles` are accepted legacy fields with no discovery
effect. All resolved top-level roles are discoverable; children stay private to
their owning role tree. Do not use those fields to publish a child.

The current YAML loader does not retain `notifications` or `extensions`, even
though programmatic role types expose them. See [Runtime features](runtime.md)
for effective notification configuration and the extension limitation.

`{env:VARIABLE_NAME}` is substituted in string values at load time, including
prompt files. Missing variables stay as placeholders. Keep credentials in the
environment or host credential store; do not print resolved secrets.

Model strings split at the first `/`: `example-provider/family/model-name`
keeps `family/model-name` as the model ID. Rolebox aliases map IDs; actual provider
registration and authentication belong to the harness.

## Tools and permissions

```yaml
permission:
  allow: [read, glob, grep]
  deny: [bash]
tools:
  bash: false
```

Replace these names with exact tools registered by the host. Host permissions,
approval handling, plugin feature gates and adapter support still apply. A YAML
entry does not create a tool or grant OS access. Codex maps supported feature denials
to native-agent settings and enforces attributed-role restrictions on rolebox MCP
calls; arbitrary native per-tool policies remain unsupported. See the mapping below.

## Subagents

Inline children can share a role's directory:

```yaml
subagents:
  - name: Researcher
    description: Finds primary evidence for the assigned question.
    prompt: |
      Research the assigned question and return sources and uncertainties.
    model: example-provider/research-model
```

For private assets, create
`<role-root>/reviewer/subagents/researcher/role.yaml` with its own `skills/`,
`functions/` and `references/`. Directory children are discovered automatically.
Inline and directory children can coexist; use distinct names.

Child IDs use the parent ID plus a slug of the child's name, separated by `--`,
for example `reviewer--researcher`. Discover the actual resolved ID before
dispatching. Children are always `subagent` mode. Recursive nesting is bounded
to three levels by default.

Child names are compared by that canonical slug: case and whitespace/hyphen
variants share one identity. Later inline definitions replace earlier ones;
inline definitions take precedence over directory definitions with the same ID.

Unset `model`, `color`, `variant`, `temperature`, `top_p`, `permission`, `tools`
and `memory` inherit from the parent. An explicit child value replaces the
parent value for that field; a partial `memory` block is not a deep merge.
Prompts, skill/function lists, `auto_activate` and `locked` do not inherit.
Default built-in functions are resolved separately for each child.

## Codex role mapping

`rolebox sync codex` exports public top-level roles as native agents. For a role ID
`reviewer`, the ordinary native name is `rolebox--reviewer`; unusual IDs use a stable
sanitized name with a digest suffix. Native files carry `name`, `description` and
`developer_instructions`, plus supported model and feature settings. Sync preserves
user edits and unmanaged collisions. Restart Codex to refresh its agent catalog.

Private children keep canonical IDs such as `reviewer--researcher` and in-memory
prompt/model/resource descriptors. They are excluded from native global discovery.
A role may target its direct children in `graph_declare`; another role or an
unattributed root conversation cannot target those children. Native `spawn_agent`
discovery alone does not publish private rolebox children. The resolver retains
deeper nested descriptors, but graph workers cannot recursively dispatch and those
deeper private descendants have no general launch path in this integration.

Bare native model IDs map directly. A `provider/model` maps only when its provider
matches the effective inherited Codex provider. Sync cannot infer that provider and
omits a qualified override with a warning, while managed graph execution reads the
parent's provider. Use a Codex alias resolving to a bare native ID when generating
native files. The adapter never overrides the provider or installs credentials.

`variant` maps to `model_reasoning_effort` for `none`, `minimal`, `low`, `medium`,
`high`, `xhigh`, `max` and `ultra`, subject to the selected model's support. Managed
workers inherit the parent's effort when no role variant is set. Other variants,
`temperature` and `top_p` are omitted with warnings.

Native files only reduce supported feature groups. A false `tools` entry or
matching `permission.deny` can disable shell (`shell_tool`, `bash`, `shell`,
`exec_command` or `write_stdin`), apps, plugins, memories (`memories` or
`memory_tool`), or permission requests (`request_permissions_tool`). These settings
cannot enable a capability disabled by the parent, widen sandbox/approval policy,
or provide arbitrary native per-tool enforcement.
Native feature denials also match trailing-star permission patterns; a matching
`permission.deny` takes precedence over an explicit `tools` grant for that alias.

For rolebox MCP calls, the host's thread identity resolves the native `agentRole`
back to its canonical role. A stale generated role is refused until sync/restart.
`permission.deny` wins; the `tools` map uses an exact name before the longest
matching trailing-star rule, and otherwise allows the tool. These restrictions
apply to rolebox's own tools, including browser/desktop tools, independently of
global registration gates. A graph worker's dedicated `graph_submit_outcome`
channel remains available; it does not grant graph control or recursive dispatch.

## Memory

```yaml
memory:
  inject: true
  max_inject: 10
  min_relevance: medium
  scope: both
  session_focus: true
  recall: true
  recall_mode: auto
```

| Setting | Default and allowed values |
| --- | --- |
| `inject` | `true`; include memory summaries in the prompt |
| `max_inject` | `10`; integer 0–100 |
| `min_relevance` | `medium`; `low`, `medium`, `high` |
| `scope` | `both`; `role`, `workspace`, `both` |
| `session_focus` | `true`; DSH session focus across compaction |
| `recall` | `true`; DSH relevant-memory search for each human prompt |
| `recall_mode` | `auto`; `auto`, `always`, `deterministic` |

`auto` adds a one-shot query scout only when workspace memory has at least 20
entries and deterministic search finds fewer than two. `always` scouts each new
human prompt; `deterministic` never scouts. Other hosts do not implement these
DSH-specific prompt blocks.

`inject: false` or `max_inject: 0` disables automatic summaries, not the memory
tools. `memory_write`, `memory_recall`, `memory_list`, `memory_read` and
`memory_update` operate within the caller's allowed workspace/role scope.
Add `functions: [memory]` for optional consolidation instructions where function
activation is supported. In DSH, request consolidation directly instead of
assuming `|memory|` activates instructions. A memory setting never grants tools
that the parent or host has denied.

Persistent entries live in the workspace's `.rolebox/memory.db`. A `workspace`
entry is shared across roles in that workspace; a `role` entry stays associated
with its role. With no active role, write workspace memories explicitly.

# Runtime features

## Browser and desktop gates

Global gates live in `<rolebox-config-home>/config.yaml`; project gates live in
`<workspace>/.rolebox/config.json`. DSH also exposes host plugin options. Any
explicit `false` or invalid/unreadable configuration disables that family at
startup; an enablement elsewhere cannot override the veto.

```yaml
computerUse: false
browseUse: false
```

Computer tools are available by default, subject to host and OS permissions.
`computer_status` diagnoses availability and `computer_permissions` checks or
requests OS permissions. Enabling the family does not confer OS permission.

For multiple windows, discover current IDs with `computer_windows`, use
`computer_focus` to bring a window forward for observation, then capture a
fresh image with `computer_screenshot`. All six input tools (`computer_click`,
`computer_move`, `computer_type`, `computer_key`, `computer_scroll` and
`computer_drag`) accept optional `window_id` on macOS, Windows and Linux X11.
Each targeted call focuses and verifies the selected window before sending
input within the same helper command and process-local queue slot. A missing,
ambiguous or refused target stops the operation. Repeat `window_id` on each
call; no selection persists, and omitting it uses the current desktop focus.
Windows discovery includes multiple visible top-level windows per process.

For example, call `computer_type` with `{"window_id":42,"text":"Example"}`
after observing window 42. Targeting brings a window forward; it does not
provide background input or lock out external focus changes. Pointer positions
remain absolute screen coordinates unless `screenshot_id` is supplied;
`window_id` does not
translate or constrain them. Use fresh coordinates inside the target window.
For targeted scrolling, supply both `x` and `y` to place the pointer; omitting
them scrolls at its current position. Windows and X11 window captures copy
visible screen content, including covering windows; X11 excludes decorations.
Focus first and verify the UI after each action. These arguments need no additional role
configuration; restart the host after updating rolebox to load the new schemas.

For multiple monitors, call `computer_displays` for current IDs, bounds, names,
UI scales and primary flags. IDs are 1-based on macOS and 0-based on Windows
and X11; refresh them after changing the display layout. X11 lists RandR
monitors on the current `DISPLAY` screen, not independent X screens. Its
default capture uses the primary monitor, or the first if none is primary.

Every successful `computer_screenshot` returns `screenshot_id`,
`screen_bounds: {x,y,w,h}`, `origin`, `pixel_scale_x`, `pixel_scale_y`, and
`displays`. A uniform ratio is also exposed as `pixel_scale`. Ratios come from
the actual PNG size and captured geometry, including fractional scales and
negative origins. Display UI scale is separate: Windows and X11 input uses
desktop/root pixels (X11 reports scale 1), while macOS uses global screen points.
macOS window capture preserves the native raster and reports its per-axis
ratios to the window bounds. Region/display
capture composites separate monitor intersections onto a uniform canvas, so
global regions may span monitors with different scales.

Pass `{"screenshot_id":"<returned id>","x":100,"y":60}` to `computer_click`
or `computer_move` to use image pixels. `computer_drag` maps both endpoints;
`computer_scroll` requires both coordinates with an ID. The captured window is
selected automatically; any explicit `window_id` must match that window.
Display/region screenshots cannot be combined with `window_id`. Outside-image
points and monitor gaps are refused. Without an ID, coordinates keep their
absolute-screen meaning. Manual conversion is `origin.x + image_x /
pixel_scale_x` and `origin.y + image_y / pixel_scale_y`.

Capture verifies geometry before and after the image. Input with an ID checks
it again after focus: moving/resizing a captured window or changing display
bounds, order, identities or scales requires a fresh screenshot. Recapturing
after a cross-monitor move uses the new origin and scale; stale UI positions
are never silently rebased. IDs are session/workspace/platform scoped, expire
after ten minutes, and the host retains at most 64; restart clears them. This
does not freeze the desktop or detect scrolling/content changes within an
unchanged frame. Observe the UI again after each action.

macOS captures use the built-in `screencapture` through JXA. Window captures
exclude shadows and preserve native raster resolution; display/region captures
compose individual monitor tiles onto a uniform logical canvas. X11 geometry needs `xrandr`
with RandR 1.5 plus `awk`; window geometry also uses `xdotool`. X11 targets must
fit inside the current root screen. Wayland remains unsupported.

Browser tools default to auto-detecting optional Playwright from the rolebox
installation. `browseUse: true` registers them even if the driver is missing so
`browse_status` can explain the gap; `false` disables them. A project dependency
that the rolebox package cannot resolve is insufficient. Use the status tool's
installation guidance rather than assuming the browser executable is present.
These settings are global/project/host options, not `role.yaml` fields.

`browse_eval` runs `expression` in the selected page without automatically waiting
for DOM elements or retrying failures. Its `metadata.code` distinguishes
`script_error` (an identifiable JavaScript exception or rejected Promise) from
`execution_context_destroyed` (navigation or frame detachment), `browser_closed`,
`timeout`, `cancelled`, and `protocol_error` (driver/protocol or unrecognized
failures). Script exceptions are identified by JavaScript error prefixes or page
execution frames; ambiguous errors such as thrown primitives without those
markers remain `protocol_error`. For script errors, fix syntax or page globals;
for null/undefined access, confirm the page and selector with `browse_snapshot`,
wait with `browse_wait`, and guard missing values. Navigation interruptions need
a fresh page observation after navigation finishes. Script errors leave the page
open; timeout/cancellation closes it, so reopen with `browse_open`. Raising
`timeout_ms` does not fix a synchronous script exception. Reserve `browse_status`
for driver availability or persistent protocol failures. This behavior applies
to every harness exposing `browse_eval`; restart the host after updating rolebox.

## Hooks and recovery

Codex's app-server adapter observes events only for managed worker threads. It does
not install rolebox's `chat.message`, native tool-interception or idle hooks into
UI-owned Codex conversations, and it does not install PluginCore hot reload,
extensions, recovery or a role switcher. Native-agent files and graph execution do
not change that boundary.

Declare custom hooks in `role.yaml`:

```yaml
hooks:
  builtin:
    session_error: true
    bash_file_read_guard: false
  custom:
    - name: quality-check
      description: Check changed files after an edit.
      events: [tool.execute.after]
      module: hooks/quality-check.js
      filter:
        tools: [edit, write, hashline_edit]
      priority: 50
      phase: after
      config:
        severity: warn
```

Hook modules resolve relative to the role directory or from an absolute path.
They use named exports `onChatMessage(ctx, input)`, `onToolBefore(ctx, input)`,
`onToolAfter(ctx, input)`, `onSystemTransform(ctx, input)` and/or
`onEvent(ctx, input)`. Optional `onLoad(ctx)` and `onDispose(ctx)` manage
lifecycle. For example, `hooks/quality-check.js` can export:

```javascript
export async function onToolAfter(ctx, input) {
  if (input.output == null) ctx.inject("The edit returned no output; verify the file before continuing.");
}
```

Supported events are `chat.message`,
`tool.execute.before`, `tool.execute.after`, `system.transform`, and `event`.
`filter.tools` selects tool names, `filter.eventTypes` selects event subtypes.
Lower priorities run earlier; default is 50. Phase is `before` or `after`
built-ins, default `after`. A hook failure is logged independently.

Known `hooks.builtin` keys:

| Default | Keys |
| --- | --- |
| Enabled | `session_error`, `edit_error`, `json_error`, `context_window`, `empty_response` |
| Disabled | `tool_pair_validation`, `write_existing_file_guard`, `bash_file_read_guard`, `webfetch_redirect_guard` |
| Enabled master switch | `recovery` |

Unknown keys warn and have no effect. Loaded roles' flags are combined by the
service; do not assume the block is an isolated per-call policy.

Recovery chain options belong under `hooks.recovery`, not a root `recovery` key:

```yaml
hooks:
  recovery:
    enabled: true
    max_total_attempts: 10
    persist_state: true
    collect_metrics: true
    edit_error:
      chain:
        - strategy: remind_and_retry
          config:
            max_retries: 2
            reminder_text: Re-read the changed file before retrying the edit.
```

Chain categories include `session_error`, `context_window`, `edit_error`,
`json_error`, `empty_response`, `tool_pair`, `guard_violation`. Known strategies
are `retry`, `compact`, `fallback_model`, `abort`, `remind_and_retry`, `truncate`
and `summarize`. Strategies need host support for their action. With multiple
roles, the service uses the first supplied recovery configuration; configure a
consistent policy rather than relying on role discovery order. Disabling
`hooks.builtin.recovery` prevents creating the recovery engine.

## Copilot continuation

Copilot is opt-in per root role:

```yaml
copilot:
  enabled: true
  rules:
    - id: wait-for-user
      match:
        contains: waiting for user input
      action: skip
    - id: continue-work
      match:
        contains: work remains
      action: continue
      reply: Continue the authorized task and verify the result.
```

The pipeline evaluates built-in active-function continuation first, ordered
Copilot rules second, and an optional LLM verdict last. First matching rule
wins; `pattern` is a regex and `contains` is case-insensitive. If both are
present they must both match. `skip` consumes the decision with no injection or
LLM fallback; `continue`, `blocked` and `done` inject their reply/default reply.
Disabling Copilot leaves built-in function continuation in place.

An optional `copilot.llm` block names a resolved private subagent:

```yaml
copilot:
  enabled: true
  llm:
    role: reviewer--continuation-judge
    max_verdict_timeout_ms: 30000
    transcript:
      window_size: 20
      max_chars: 8000
      include_tools: true
```

Create that judge subagent before enabling this block. `guidance`, if supplied,
replaces the default advisory guidance entirely. The judge uses a fresh child
session; unknown role, timeout or failed verdict skips the LLM decision without
retry. Copilot requires host idle/message hooks and is not installed into native
Codex conversations by the MCP server.

## Codex session and worker runtime

The six Codex session tools browse native threads through app-server, with
workspace filtering and paginated turns/items. `session_diff` shows recorded file
patches. `session_fork` requires host sandbox metadata and a completed turn boundary:
use a turn ID or that turn's final message ID, never a message in the middle of a
turn. Live todos and execution state require events from an app-server this adapter
owns; another process's thread may report `notLoaded` here and remains unknown.
Token/cost telemetry is not supplied by this adapter.

Fatal transport failure rejects pending calls and terminates the app-server process
tree. MCP close, `SIGINT` and `SIGTERM` also clean up managed descendants. These
local actions do not establish a native turn outcome: absent a terminal event, the
execution remains unknown. The adapter does not automatically restart the transport
or retry a worker.

Per-call `_meta.threadId` supplies thread identity; `_meta.sessionId` may be shared
by forks and is not a worker identity. Legacy connection identity remains usable
for standalone tools but cannot execute graph tools. Native role attribution reads
the thread's `agentRole`; attributed roles narrow rolebox tool calls. Global
browser/desktop gates still control registration, and OS permissions still apply.

The MCP `ask()` callback remains unavailable for standalone tools. Managed graph
workers reject fresh interactive approval/input requests and use native task tools
inside the inherited sandbox. Their outer-process dynamic face contains only
outcome submission and allowed scoped resource reads. They do not receive
`hashline_edit`, interactive terminal, desktop or browser tools through that face.
Cancellation during a pending turn start is queued until the turn ID arrives;
`requested` is distinct from Codex's interrupted confirmation. A positive node
`timeout_ms` includes launch time, records timeout control for the exact attempt and
requests interruption. Zero disables the watchdog, and expiry never retries work.
See [Orchestration](orchestration.md#codex-execution) for graph result collection,
cancellation and restart behavior.

## Notifications

Set `ROLEBOX_NOTIFICATIONS_CONFIG` to a YAML file containing the notification
block directly, without a `notifications:` wrapper:

```yaml
enabled: true
mainSessionOnly: true
idleDelayMs: 1500
channels:
  - kind: system_toast
    enabled: true
events:
  approval_pending:
    enabled: true
  idle:
    enabled: false
quietHours:
  enabled: true
  timezone: Asia/Shanghai
  ranges:
    - start: "23:00"
      end: "08:00"
throttle:
  windowMs: 3000
  maxPerWindow: 3
```

Global defaults enable notifications but supply no channels. Channel kinds are
`system_toast`, `sound` (`soundPath`), `custom_command` (`command`, optional
`passAsStdin`, `env`), `webhook` (`url`, optional `headers`, `timeoutMs`), `file`
(`path`) and `log` (optional `level`). Keep URLs/headers with credentials in
environment placeholders such as `{env:NOTIFICATION_URL}`. Configure external
delivery only within the user's requested scope.

Events include `idle`, `question`, `permission`, `error`, `dispatch_complete`,
`dispatch_progress`, `loop_complete`, `approval_pending`, `session_deleted` and
custom names. Per-event settings include `enabled`, `channels`, `titleTemplate`,
`messageTemplate`, `throttle` and `quietHoursOverride`. `questionToolNames`
customizes detection. A quiet-hours range can specify `days: [Mon, Tue]`.
`ROLEBOX_NOTIFICATIONS_ENABLED=false` or `0` disables the global configuration.

Programmatic role notification configuration replaces scalar defaults and the
channel list, merging events by key. The current YAML role loader drops a
`notifications:` field, so use the global file for file-authored roles. Do not
claim a per-role YAML notification override will work in this version.

## Extensions

The extension registry supports custom conditions, graph topologies, recovery
strategies/patterns, notification channels and observe events. It is additive;
module failures are logged and skipped. However, the current YAML role loader
does not retain `extensions`, so merely adding an `extensions:` block to a role
file does not register modules. A working programmatic integration is required.
Do not invent a file configuration workaround or edit rolebox internals as part
of an ordinary configuration task; explain this limitation if the user needs it.

## LSP

OpenCode, Pi and DSH expose the same 32 `lsp_*` tools. The Codex integration does
not expose this family. Rolebox selects the server by file extension and starts
it on the first file operation; the server reads the workspace's project
configuration. Servers are not installed automatically. Put the relevant
executable on the host process's `PATH`:

| Languages | Executable |
| --- | --- |
| TypeScript / JavaScript | `typescript-language-server` |
| Python | `pyright-langserver` |
| Go | `gopls` |
| Rust | `rust-analyzer` |
| C / C++ | `clangd` |
| Java | `jdtls` |
| Ruby | `solargraph` |
| Shell | `bash-language-server` |
| Lua | `lua-language-server` |
| Kotlin | `kotlin-lsp` |

There is no general `lsp:` block in `role.yaml`. Install/configure the server
through its own supported mechanisms, then restart the host if its environment
was changed. TypeScript/JavaScript also needs a TypeScript installation that
`typescript-language-server` can resolve.

On DSH the family is enabled by default. `enabledNamespaces: ["lsp"]` registers
only LSP tools; `["*", "!lsp"]` excludes them. Exact names such as `lsp_hover`
also work. This is the normal plugin namespace filter, not an LSP-specific
setting. A host-owned name uses the usual `rb_` collision fallback (for example
`rb_lsp_hover`); use the names actually discovered in the session. Restart DSH
after changing the plugin's registration settings.

DSH keeps separate language-server processes, open documents and diagnostic
caches per session workspace. The host working-directory service takes
precedence, then the latest `working-directory/change` event, then the session
header's `cwd`; calls without session workspace metadata fall back to the
process working directory. Sessions in the same workspace share its servers.
The service tracks sessions that have used LSP. Changing one of those sessions'
workspaces transfers its reference; `session/disposed` releases it. When the last
such session leaves a workspace, it is retired immediately, even if no further
tool is called. Accepted calls finish on that generation before its documents,
diagnostic state and child processes are closed. Other sessions using the same
workspace keep their shared servers. Calls without a known session retain a
workspace only while their calls are in flight. Plugin unload releases all
remaining workspaces and waits for their cleanup.

Cleanup drains accepted calls first; ordinary LSP requests can each take up to
30 seconds to time out. The shutdown request has a separate two-second deadline,
followed by SIGTERM and, if the process remains alive for another two seconds,
SIGKILL. This bounds shutdown negotiation, not the total time spent draining a
tool that performs several requests. Failed or timed-out initialization also
awaits this termination sequence before another start can use that language.
Three consecutive startup failures require `lsp_restart_server`; a successful
initialization resets the failure count, so healthy restarts do not accumulate
past crashes. In-flight requests are cancelled when their server shuts down.

Start with `lsp_servers` to inspect discovery without launching a process, then
call `lsp_hover` or `lsp_diagnostics` with an absolute project file path. For
example, `lsp_hover` accepts:

```json
{"filePath":"/path/to/project/src/index.ts","line":0,"character":0}
```

Positions are zero-based UTF-16 line/character offsets. Document synchronization,
requests and diagnostic caches use the same canonical file URI, including
Windows drives, UNC paths and reserved filename characters. Equivalent file URI
encodings returned by a server are normalized before diagnostics are cached.

File diagnostics use pull diagnostics when advertised, otherwise they wait for
the server's publication after synchronization. The initial read has a five-second
budget. A missing result is reported as unavailable, without claiming the file
is clean. For the same document version, another wait is suppressed for 30 seconds;
a publication is visible immediately, and an edit, restart or cooldown expiry
allows a new attempt. Quickfix tools wait for current diagnostics before building
their context; if diagnostics remain unavailable, the context is explicitly empty.
Closing a document removes its cached diagnostics and ignores late publications.
Without `filePath`,
`lsp_diagnostics` reads the workspace's cached diagnostics. `lsp_workspace_symbols`
queries servers already started in that workspace, so use a file tool first.
`lsp_restart_server` takes a detected `languageId` such as `typescript`; the next
file call reopens its document in the replacement process.

Individual operations depend on the server's advertised capabilities. An
unsupported operation reports that limitation. Capabilities are negotiated at
initialization; dynamic capability registration is not implemented or advertised.
Rename returns an edit preview;
formatting and execute-code-action tools can write files. Use host logs for
discovery, startup and protocol failures.

DSH graph workers inherit parent-authorized LSP tools, including the file-writing
`lsp_format_document`, `lsp_format_range` and `lsp_execute_code_action` tools.
There is no additional default LSP write gate. To exclude these from the inherited
worker catalog, set `tools` on the acting parent role, for example:

```yaml
tools:
  lsp_format_document: false
  lsp_format_range: false
  lsp_execute_code_action: false
```

These policies also match `rb_` collision aliases by their canonical names.
Node `tools` lists are legacy metadata and cannot grant a denied tool; native,
discovery and code presentation use the same inherited authorization.
